reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: collection.upsertEntity(row) — a key this population has never seen
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR DOES LESS, AND KNOWABLY SO. Ours mints an identity (a slot and an entry in the identity store — there is no per-index `links` cell, so a row carries nothing per index at all), copies the row, walks the copy's own names to refuse the ones a row may not carry, stamps the slot, stamps the collection and records the row on the presence channel so every index and every whole-population reader hears about it. The floor allocates one copy and hashes one string. Direction: this inflates our ratio, and no three-line floor can close the gap — what the extra buys is that anything subscribed to this population, or indexing it, is woken by this insert. The tracked row below is the closest a few lines get. Both sides abandon their container between passes and both are collected outside the clock, so the GC of what each allocated is NOT inside either number; our allocation per row is roughly three objects to the floor's one, and that debt is paid later.

reading.floor: const row = map.get(id); if (row !== undefined) row.title = value
reading.caveat: THE ONE WRITE ROW WHERE BOTH SIDES PAY THE LOOKUP, which is what makes it the fair comparison for a key that arrived from outside. Ours is one map read and then the identity path priced two rows up; the floor is one map read and a store. The difference between this ratio and the update.column ratio is the price of NOT having held the identity — the engine's own source puts that at 103-132 ns against 36-51 [NO RUN BEHIND THIS FIGURE], and this row is the independent check on that claim.

reading.floor: const row = map.get(id); if (row !== undefined) row.title = value
reading.caveat: The column door by key: no patch object and no walk over one. Both sides pay the lookup; ours then compares the value, writes it in place and marks the entity changed once per frame.

reading.ours: collection.clearContent(slot) — through the identity, no index registered
reading.caveat: THE HASH IS ON THE FLOOR'S SIDE ONLY: ours is handed the identity and the floor hashes a string, which flatters us — the deleteEntityByKey path is not priced here and would cost us that lookup too. Against that, ours clears the value through the writer, reports it on the channel, recomputes emptiness and asks whether anything holds or references the identity before it unfiles it from the store — an unheld, emptied slot is released at the call. The flush that closes the batch is inside the timed body. The floor's row is gone the instant delete returns and nothing can be subscribed to it. Both sides rebuild their population between passes, untimed.

reading.ours: collection.findEntityByKey(id) — the entity of a key, or undefined
reading.caveat: THE CALIBRATION ROW. `findEntityByKey` is `findSlotByKey` — one call into the slot store service and one `Map.get` — and one `.entity` load off the slot, so if this reads much above 1 the instrument is measuring call overhead rather than the library, and every other ratio in this table should be read with that in mind. Every key hits — a miss is a different path on both sides and would mix two prices.

Ours is two calls deep — the bucket collection hands the question to its bucket slots service, whose `size` reads the same `Set.size` — and those two calls are the whole difference. The floor reads a field of a container whose correctness is somebody else's problem. Both sides cycle through all sixty-four buckets rather than asking the same one repeatedly. THIS ROW ONCE READ BELOW 1.00 AND THAT NUMBER WAS A HASH, NOT A COUNT. The floor reached its `Set` through `sets.get(name)` — a string-keyed `Map.get` — while our side was handed the bucket out of an array. So the floor's number was very nearly all addressing and ours was very nearly all service hop, and the row reported the difference between a hash and an array load under the name of a member count. The floor now holds its sets in an array indexed exactly the way our side indexes its buckets, so both sides are addressed alike and what is left in the ratio is the service hop. This suite's standing rule is that a floor doing less is a lie in our favour; that rule was pointed at us here, and the reading it produced is withdrawn rather than qualified. THE CALL WAS `db.memberCount(bucket)` AND IS `bucketCollection.getBucketMemberSlotCount(bucket)`, on the bucket collection rather than on the database — the same question through a different object. Nothing recorded before 2026-08-29 is re-attributed to it, and the prediction the old caveat carried (roughly 3.5 to 4.4, from figures in `measurements/2026-08-20-price/read-2`) was written for the old call and is not a prediction about this one.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntityByKey(id, patch), flush, and the subscription fires — per key delivered
reading.floor: map.get(id) and store the field, add the id to a Set of changed ids, and at flush call every handler a Map of id → handlers holds for each changed id
reading.caveat: Both sides address the entity by its string key on every write and deliver once per flush. Ours resolves the key to the slot and then reaches the subscribers through `slot.effects`; the floor resolves the key twice, once to the row and once at flush to its handlers. One write per key per frame, a thousand keys, one subscriber each. The floor holds only for a one-column write that nothing but the subscriber listens to.
